description.summary: OpenSearch is an open-source distributed search and analytics engine with native exact, approximate, filtered, sparse, neural, and hybrid vector retrieval.
description.description: OpenSearch combines Lucene-based lexical search and analytics with configurable k-nearest-neighbor vector fields, Lucene and Faiss ANN engines, HNSW and IVF methods, vector quantization, efficient filtering, neural sparse retrieval, and search-pipeline-based hybrid fusion. It runs locally or in self-managed clusters and is available through Amazon OpenSearch Service and OpenSearch Serverless. This record distinguishes open-source engine capabilities from AWS-managed deployment guarantees and from algorithm-, version-, and workload-dependent performance behavior.

indexingConsiderations: Choose Lucene or Faiss, HNSW or IVF, vector dimensions, spaces, workload mode, and quantization only after measuring recall, latency, memory, disk, ingestion, and build cost.
Plan primary shards, replicas, node roles, allocation domains, recovery capacity, and shard size before large-scale ingestion.
Use explicit mappings and index templates for vector, text, sparse, and metadata fields rather than relying on accidental dynamic mappings.
Treat open-source, Amazon managed-domain, and serverless index settings as separate compatibility targets.
retrievalConsiderations: Evaluate BM25-only, dense-vector, neural-sparse, and hybrid retrieval on the same relevance set.
Place efficient filters inside supported k-NN queries when top-k filtered recall matters and distinguish them from post-filtering.
Tune k, candidate counts, HNSW or IVF parameters, normalization, fusion weights, rank constants, and reranking under representative load.
Profile shard-level execution and coordinating-node pipeline costs separately.

limitations: OpenSearch is a broad search and analytics platform, so its schema, cluster, plugin, and operational surface is larger than that of a dedicated vector database.
ANN engines, algorithms, quantization, compression, and on-disk modes trade recall and indexing cost for memory, storage, and query efficiency.
Filter placement changes execution strategy and top-k guarantees; post-filtering can return fewer than the requested neighbors.
Hybrid search depends on search pipelines, candidate windows, normalization, fusion, model quality, and coordinating-node resources.
Shard count, replica placement, recovery, segment merges, caches, and hot spots can materially affect performance and resilience.
Amazon OpenSearch Service and Serverless expose deployment-specific quotas, pricing, supported APIs, plugins, regions, and operational behavior.
Search visibility is near-real-time and can lag acknowledged writes until refresh.
OpenSearch does not provide general relational-style multi-document ACID transactions.
usageGuidance: Record OpenSearch, Lucene, plugin, client, and model versions because vector defaults, APIs, algorithms, and search-pipeline behavior change across releases.
Benchmark the exact engine, algorithm, compression, shard topology, filter selectivity, query mix, and hardware intended for production.
Use snapshots and restore drills for disaster recovery; replicas improve availability but do not replace backups.
Monitor cluster and shard health, refresh and merge pressure, vector-memory usage, native-library caches, disk watermarks, latency, recall, and hybrid relevance.
Review managed-service compatibility and security boundaries before moving between self-hosted, provisioned, and serverless deployments.

claims.statement: OpenSearch stores dense vectors in knn_vector fields and supports exact and approximate k-nearest-neighbor retrieval using Lucene, Faiss, and deprecated NMSLIB engines with HNSW, IVF, in-memory or on-disk modes, multiple distance spaces, and built-in vector quantization.
claims.rationale: The OpenSearch vector-search documentation describes exact and ANN techniques, engine and algorithm choices, vector workload modes, distance spaces, and scalar, product, byte, and binary quantization options.

claims.statement: OpenSearch supports efficient filtered approximate k-NN search with Lucene HNSW and Faiss HNSW or IVF, while post-filter and scoring-script alternatives have different top-k, recall, and latency behavior.

qualifiers.name: filterScope
qualifiers.value: Filter semantics depend on engine, algorithm, placement, selectivity, and exact-versus-approximate execution

claims.rationale: The filtering documentation distinguishes efficient candidate-stage filtering from Boolean or post_filter post-filtering and from exact scoring-script filtering.

claims.statement: OpenSearch hybrid search combines keyword, neural, dense-vector, and sparse retrieval through search pipelines that support score normalization and weighted combination or rank-based Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

qualifiers.name: relevanceScope
qualifiers.value: Normalization, fusion, weights, rank constants, candidate sizes, models, and filters require workload-specific evaluation

claims.rationale: The hybrid-search and search-pipeline documentation describes score-based normalization and combination as well as weighted RRF over multiple query clauses.

claims.statement: OpenSearch distributes indexes across primary and replica shards and can be deployed locally or self-hosted, while Amazon OpenSearch Service provides managed domains and an auto-scaling serverless option including vector-search collections.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Self-hosted OpenSearch and Amazon managed or serverless offerings expose different operational controls, limits, APIs, and responsibility boundaries

claims.rationale: OpenSearch documents primary and replica shard distribution, and AWS documents managed and serverless OpenSearch configurations with automatic capacity management.

claims.statement: OpenSearch routes document writes to a primary shard and its active replicas, provides document-level versioning and optimistic concurrency control, and offers near-real-time search visibility rather than general multi-document ACID transactions.

qualifiers.name: consistencyScope
qualifiers.value: Write acknowledgement, active replicas, refresh behavior, shard health, and concurrency parameters affect durability and visibility

claims.rationale: The document API documentation describes primary-replica write propagation, versioning, sequence numbers, primary terms, and the distinction between real-time document access and refresh-dependent search visibility.

evidence.summary: Official OpenSearch sources document knn_vector storage, exact and approximate search, Lucene and Faiss engines, HNSW and IVF methods, on-disk mode, multiple spaces, and several quantization approaches.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent OpenSearch as a search engine with broad vector-index configuration rather than as a dedicated vector database.

sourceFragments.locator: knn_vector modes, spaces, and method definitions

limitations: Official documentation establishes supported functionality but is not an independent performance benchmark.
Engine, algorithm, compression, mode, dimension, hardware, filters, and query parameters materially affect recall and latency.

evidence.summary: OpenSearch documents efficient filtering during ANN search for Lucene HNSW and Faiss HNSW or IVF, alongside post-filter and exact scoring-script alternatives.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark metadata filtering as supported while warning that filter placement and selectivity alter top-k guarantees and execution strategy.

sourceFragments.locator: Lucene and Faiss efficient filtering algorithms and comparison with post-filtering and scoring scripts

limitations: Highly selective filters can trigger exact-search fallbacks or additional graph traversal.
Post-filtering may return substantially fewer than k results even when enough matching documents exist globally.

evidence.summary: OpenSearch hybrid queries use search pipelines to normalize and combine keyword and semantic scores or to apply weighted RRF over ranked result lists.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark BM25-plus-vector, sparse-dense fusion, weighted score fusion, and RRF as supported hybrid patterns.
limitations: Fusion quality depends on query sets, judgment lists, candidate counts, normalization, and model quality.
Search-pipeline and hybrid-query feature combinations have version-specific restrictions and coordinating-node costs.

evidence.summary: OpenSearch documents primary and replica shard distribution, while Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides auto-scaling managed collections including vector-search workloads.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high horizontal scalability and multiple deployment models while separating open-source engine behavior from AWS-managed service guarantees.

sourceFragments.locator: Primary and replica shards and cluster scaling guidance
Serverless auto-scaling, availability, encryption, and capacity management

limitations: Shard count, allocation, recovery, and hot spots remain workload-sensitive in self-hosted clusters.
Managed and serverless limits, pricing, supported APIs, plugins, regions, and lifecycle behavior differ from self-hosted OpenSearch.

evidence.summary: OpenSearch document APIs describe primary-replica write propagation, version increments, optimistic concurrency fields, and refresh-dependent search visibility.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark document-level transaction semantics and configurable consistency without claiming relational multi-document ACID transactions.

sourceFragments.locator: Document write replication, versioning, optimistic concurrency, and refresh behavior

limitations: Acknowledged writes and real-time GET behavior do not imply immediate visibility in ordinary search results before refresh.
Bulk and update-by-query operations can partially succeed and do not provide atomic rollback across multiple documents.
